clue.text: Request millions during sample TV programme

indicators.note: 'during' puts a thing inside the stretch of time it names, so these letters go within the word that follows rather than beside it.

blocks.note: to ask for something is to request it
m is the standard abbreviation for millions, as in a salary quoted at 3m
a taster is a sample, the small portion handed out to try

explanation.surface: Asking for millions while a trial episode is on the screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sample' is the small helping handed round, not the pilot episode the surface offers. The show is named for the stern figure who hands out the tasks.
explanation.definitionFit: Taskmaster is the Channel 4 comedy in which comedians attempt absurd tasks, so the definition names the answer by example.

clue.text: Heavy metal style pants will suit husband

indicators.note: a thing that will suit someone takes them in and fits round them, so the letter named next sits inside.

blocks.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, which is trash
h is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Heavy metal trousers that the husband could get away with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is the British adjective for useless rather than the trousers the surface hangs on the husband. Thrash is the fast, aggressive corner of heavy metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrash metal, played at speed with shouted vocals, is one recognised style within heavy metal.

clue.text: Small drink to follow spiel

blocks.note: s is the clothing-label abbreviation for small
ale is the crossword's shortest drink
to stalk someone is to follow them

explanation.surface: A small drink lined up for after the speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The join hides the break: the two words of the answer divide one letter later than the three pieces of the wordplay do.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiel is the practised patter a salesman reels off to shift something, which is sales talk exactly.

clue.text: Restaurants want these snails trim, and chef mostly performs

definitions.note: The definition is a clause naming the answer by who covets it rather than a synonym; 'these' stands in for the plural the grid wants.

indicators.note: 'mostly' keeps most of a word and no more, so the last letter of the word beside it never arrives.
to perform is to act a thing out rather than be it, and letters acting out come on in an order other than the printed one.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder
CHEF without its last letter, the three letters that complete the thirteen

explanation.surface: A restaurant wanting its snails neat and its chef on song most nights.
explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters of fodder lie in the open while the definition passes for the start of an ordinary sentence. The Michelin Guide is the tyre firm's restaurant book, and its stars are the trade's top honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Michelin stars are the ratings the Michelin Guide awards, and one of them turns a kitchen into a destination, which is why restaurants chase them.

clue.text: Employee who's lacking secretarial skill

blocks.note: to be short of something is to lack it
a hand is a worker - a farm hand, all hands on deck

explanation.surface: A member of staff who cannot take dictation.
explanation.walkthrough: The employee comes first in the clue and second in the answer, so the pieces have to be read out of order. Pitman and Teeline are the systems a secretary learns.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorthand is the symbol writing that keeps up with speech, taught for taking dictation in an office.

clue.text: Upright before court

blocks.note: ere is the old word for before
ct is the abbreviation for court, the one used on street signs and envelopes

explanation.surface: Standing up straight ahead of a court appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: Ere survives now only in poetry and in crosswords, where it is the three letters for 'before'. The surface wants 'before court' to be the hearing, and it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means standing straight up - an erect posture, an erect column - which is what upright says of a thing.

clue.text: Switch feet to do the moonwalk?

indicators.note: the moonwalk is the dance step that travels backwards while the feet appear to walk forwards, so the letters run the other way.

blocks.note: an animal's feet are its paws

explanation.surface: Changing which foot leads in order to pull off the backwards glide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switch feet' reads as a single instruction to a dancer, and the definition stops after the first word. The feet belong to an animal, not to the performer.
explanation.definitionFit: To swap is to exchange one thing for another, the everyday sense of switch - switch seats, swap seats.

clue.text: Share defeat

blocks.note: the portion each person is down for, as in paying your own
the colloquial verb for beating a side soundly

explanation.surface: Two sides going down to the same loss together.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are colloquial and neither is signposted, so a two-word clue offers nothing but the pair of senses to work on.
explanation.definitionFit: Share -> WHACK: a whack is a portion, as in paying your whack; defeat -> WHACK: to whack a team is to beat them soundly.

clue.text: Gather this girl's not real cowgirl material?

blocks.note: a pleat is a fold gathered into cloth
her is the word for this girl once she has been mentioned

explanation.surface: A girl told her outfit would never pass on a working ranch.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight the clue opens 'I gather this girl's...', with gather as understanding rather than the fold sewn into a skirt. Pleather runs plastic and leather together.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleather is plastic made up to look like leather, so a cowgirl's jacket cut from it is not the real hide.

clue.text: Touching musical phrase nearly finished old person

indicators.note: something nearly finished stops just before its end, so the last letter of the word never gets written.

blocks.note: re means concerning, the sense of touching in 'touching the matter in hand'
a lick is the guitarist's short run of notes, here one letter short of the whole

explanation.surface: A moving piece of music almost seeing off an elderly listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks like the effect the music has and is the legal sense instead, the one crosswords shorten to two letters. Lick for a phrase comes from jazz and rock playing.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is what is left over from an earlier age, and applied to a person it is the joky word for someone who belongs to another era.

clue.text: Uninitiated beaus hurry to give inappropriate details

indicators.note: the uninitiated are the ones never let in at the start, so the word beside it loses the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: beaus are lovers, and the initial L is the letter taken off
to hare off somewhere is to hurry

explanation.surface: Boyfriends who were never in on the secret rushing to spill it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uninitiated' works twice over on the surface and in the wordplay: men not in the know, and a word without its opening letter. Hare is the verb here, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshare is to tell people more about your private life than they ever wanted to hear, which is giving details that are not appropriate.

clue.text: Impatient with gigs, reworked old puppet show

indicators.note: something reworked has been taken apart and made again differently, so the letters come back in a new order.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder
four more, thirteen in all

explanation.surface: A performer tired of touring giving an old puppet show an overhaul.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8,5 split falls nowhere near the break between the two fodder words, which is what makes thirteen letters hard to spot. Spitting Image was the ITV satire whose latex puppets mocked Thatcher's cabinet and the royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: Spitting Image is the television show whose grotesque puppets caricatured politicians through the 1980s, long enough ago to be called old.

clue.text: Dodgy American quietly infiltrates party

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside something that never invited you, so these letters slip into the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: us is the standard abbreviation for American
p is piano on a score, the instruction to play quietly
a sect is a party, a faction split off from the main body

explanation.surface: An American slipping discreetly into somebody else's party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' is the faction, not the drinks the surface pours, and the spy story it tells has nothing to do with the definition standing alone at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Something suspect is not to be trusted - suspect motives, a suspect parcel - which is what dodgy means in British usage.

clue.text: Bushes hot to disrupt party policies

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: a thicket is named here by the bushes it is made of.

indicators.note: to disrupt a thing is to break into the middle of it, so the letter lands inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: h is the tap-label abbreviation for hot
a party's ticket is the slate of candidates and policies it stands on in American elections

explanation.surface: The Bush family keen to upset their party's platform.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B at the head of the clue hides the shrubbery behind the presidential family, and 'hot to' reads as eager in the surface while only the h is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A thicket is a stand of shrubs grown so close together that there is no walking through it.

clue.text: Pursuing answer, fool had trouble

indicators.note: whatever pursues something follows along behind it, so the pieces named next line up after the first letter.

blocks.note: a is the abbreviation for answer, as on a quiz sheet
git is the British word for an idiot
had is the dining sense - he had lunch - not possession

explanation.surface: Chasing a reply, an idiot ran into difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' sits at the end where the surface wants a noun and the answer needs a verb. Pursuing is doing no letter work at all - it only says which piece leads.
explanation.definitionFit: To agitate is to stir a thing up or unsettle a person, the same job the verb trouble does - what troubles you agitates you.

clue.text: Brilliant flipping tackle by English fellow

indicators.note: to flip a thing is to turn it over, so the letters gathered before it are read back from the far end.

blocks.note: a luff is a tackle in the nautical sense, a purchase of blocks and rope
e is the standard abbreviation for English
a gent is a fellow

explanation.surface: A dazzling tackle put in by an Englishman on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brilliant' is light rather than the praise a match report would mean by it, and 'flipping' is the turning instruction rather than the mild oath. The tackle is ship's rigging, not rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: Effulgent describes something shining out brightly - an effulgent sunrise - which is brilliant in its original sense of giving off light.

clue.text: Rubbish Tesla not green anymore?

blocks.note: the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density, has the symbol T
green fruit is unripe, so fruit that is green no longer is ripe

explanation.surface: An electric car that has stopped being good for the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesla is the unit before it is the car, and green here is ripeness rather than ecology. The question mark flags that the second half needs working out rather than looking up.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is stomach lining sold as food, and the transferred sense - utter tripe - is the everyday British word for rubbish.

clue.text: Who's not so civil, entering home with tenants on vacation?

definitions.text: Who's not so civil, entering home with tenants on vacation?
definitions.note: The whole clue defines the answer, and 'who's' covers a gang as readily as one person asking the question.

indicators.note: to enter a place is to go inside it, so the letters named before it are set within the ones named after.
a house on vacation stands empty, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends and nothing in between.

blocks.note: someone at home is in
the two ends of TENANTS, everything between them emptied out
less civil than someone else is ruder, the comparative

explanation.surface: A question about who lets themselves into a house while the tenants are away.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word earns its keep twice: the question the clue asks is also the instruction that builds the answer. 'Not so civil' is a comparative, which is the step most solvers walk past.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes people who let themselves into someone else's home while the tenants are away, and civility is not their strong point.

clue.text: Lovely song and dance in front of half-hearted crowd

indicators.note: what stands in front of a thing is written before it, so this piece leads the answer.
a half-hearted word keeps only half of what is at its heart, so one of the twin letters in the middle is dropped.

blocks.note: a song and dance about something is a fuss, an ado
a crowd is a rabble, and one of the two b's at its centre goes

explanation.surface: A fuss kicked up in front of a crowd that is not really interested.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-hearted takes half the heart, not half the word: the middle of RABBLE is a double letter and half of two is one. A song and dance is the fuss you make, not the turn you put on.
explanation.definitionFit: Adorable means fit to be adored - an adorable puppy, an adorable baby - which is lovely at its warmest.

clue.text: Drunk fans periodically visited composer

indicators.note: letters visited at regular periods are called on one in every two, so every other letter is passed over.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of DRUNKFANS

explanation.surface: Tipsy supporters dropping in from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like an anagram instruction and is fodder instead, with the letters staying in the order they were printed. Dukas wrote The Sorcerer's Apprentice, the music Disney gave Mickey Mouse in Fantasia.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Dukas was a French composer of the turn of the twentieth century, best remembered for The Sorcerer's Apprentice.

clue.text: No longer able to eat lunch's contents

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a phrase, but 'a firm no longer' and 'a defunct firm' say the same thing.

indicators.note: eating a thing takes it inside you, so the letters named next finish up in the middle.
a thing's contents are what is inside it, so the letters at the two ends are left out.

blocks.note: deft hands are able ones
the inside of L-UNC-H

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot manage the rest of what is in their lunchbox.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops after two words, so 'able to eat' belongs to the wordplay and not to the picture of a full stomach the clue paints.
explanation.definitionFit: A defunct company or law has ceased to exist, so saying a thing is defunct is saying that it is no longer.

clue.text: Watch shillings coming in

blocks.note: s is the old money abbreviation for shillings, as in 4s 6d
an entry is a coming in

explanation.surface: Keeping an eye on the small change as it arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: Shillings went with decimalisation in 1971, but their s survives in wordplay. 'Coming in' has to be read as a noun, which is the switch the surface hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is the soldier posted to keep watch, and the watch is the old word for that duty and for the men who stand it.

clue.text: Gunners find continued struggles

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: the rat race is the name for the endless struggling the plural describes.

blocks.note: the Royal Artillery, whose men are the Gunners
to trace something is to find it

explanation.surface: Artillerymen discovering that the fighting has not stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: The break in the answer falls inside the wordplay's second piece, one letter after the RA. Gunners is also Arsenal's nickname, which is the other army the surface may suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the grinding competition of commuting and career, a struggle that starts again every morning.

clue.text: Leaders from Tooting and Walthamstow chill now and again

indicators.note: the leader of a name is the letter at its head, so only the opening letter of each is taken.

blocks.note: the first letters of two districts of London
ice is what you drop in a drink to chill it

explanation.surface: Tooting and Walthamstow's top brass unwinding every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now and again' reads as occasionally and counts to two when taken at its word - once now, once again. Tooting and Walthamstow are London suburbs, picked for their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken literally, now and again is one occasion plus a second one, which is the count twice makes.

clue.text: Time hard to manage when upset

indicators.note: a thing upset has been tipped over, and in a down answer that means the letters are read up the grid instead of down.

blocks.note: h is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
to cope is to manage

explanation.surface: A stretch you struggle to handle once you are distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to manage' reads as one phrase and breaks into two pieces, a letter and a verb. Upset is a reversal here because the answer runs downwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An epoch is a stretch of history - the Victorian epoch, a new epoch in science - so it is time taken in the large.

clue.text: Holiday souvenir from Hawaii in the bag

blocks.note: the flower garland hung round a visitor's neck in Hawaii
a result in the bag is a sure one

explanation.surface: A Hawaiian keepsake safely packed for the journey home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holiday souvenir' looks like one phrase and the definition is only its first word. In the bag is the idiom that gives the second piece, nothing to do with luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure and holiday both name time that belongs to you rather than to work - a life of leisure, a week's holiday.

clue.text: Hell's got this mobster in for straightening out

definitions.note: The definition is a clause rather than a noun: the answer is named by what hell is stocked with.

indicators.note: straightening a thing out pulls it about and lays it down differently, so the letters settle in another order.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder
two more, nine in all

explanation.surface: A gangster taken in for a course of reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In for' reads as a prison sentence and is two letters of fodder plus a link word. Brimstone is sulphur under its Biblical name, as in fire and brimstone.
explanation.definitionFit: Brimstone is the old name for sulphur, and the preachers' fire and brimstone is what hell is traditionally stocked with.

clue.text: Head off state tax at the outset

indicators.note: at the outset means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word is taken.

blocks.note: to aver is to state something as fact
the letter tax starts with

explanation.surface: Blocking a state tax before it can get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' is the definition, though it reads as the opening of an instruction about tax. Aver is the courtroom word for stating a thing as fact.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert a disaster is to turn it aside before it arrives, which is what heading something off means.

clue.text: First lady, Republican to the end

blocks.note: Eve, the first woman in Genesis
r is the standard abbreviation for Republican, and the clue puts it last

explanation.surface: A First Lady who stayed loyal to her party to the last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First lady' is Eve rather than a president's wife. 'To the end' earns its place twice: it says where the R goes and it is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever means for all the time there is, so keeping something up to the end is keeping it up ever after.

clue.text: Hot pose modelled for one pictorial feature

indicators.note: a thing modelled has been worked into a new shape, so the letters take a form other than the one given.

blocks.note: the seven letters of HOTPOSE in a new order
say is the word that introduces an example, as 'for one' does

explanation.surface: A model holding a sultry position for the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram runs across the hyphen and ends two letters into the second word, so the split in the answer is no guide to the split in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A photo-essay tells its story in pictures with captions at most, which is a magazine feature made of photographs.
